newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Honda's "Dream" comes true, winning solar car race.
newsitem.headline: Honda's "Dream" comes true, winning solar car race.

text.p: The Japanese Honda "Dream" car on Wednesday won the fourth World Solar Challenge, breaking race records in the tough 3,010 km (1,870 mile) sun-powered drive across Australia from Darwin to Adelaide.

The Honda car became the first to make the journey in just four days, sailing through peak-hour traffic to the finish line with an average race time of 89.76 kmph (55.77 mph), up from the previous record average of 84.96 kmph (52.79 mph).

Race officials said the Dream took 33 hours, 32 minutes for the journey, clipping more than two hours off the previous race record, held by the Honda team which won the 1993 challenge in 35 hours and 47 minutes.
Honda team leader Masashi Kitagawa told a news conference after the race he was happy with the performance of the Dream, developed at an estimated cost of A$10 million (US$7.9 million).

Race organiser Hans Tholstrup, who will now retire from the event he founded in 1987, said the world will never see its suburban roads dominated by solar-powered vehicles, but the race would lead to energy improvements in motor vehicles.

Dream, with its sleek winged form covered with monocrystal silicon cells and a top speed of 140 kmph (86.99 mph), was the race favourite in a field of 57 solar-powered cars and bicycles, valued at A$60 million, which entered this year's challenge.
Officials said Swiss car Schooler was expected to take second place early on Thursday ahead of Japan's Aisol III.
A German competitor, racing a solar bicycle, died two hours into the race on Sunday after suffering a heart attack.
Kitagawa said he hoped the triennial race would continue and that other car manufacturers would join the challenge.
"It is a race which is good for the future, so the more companies which enter the better it is for technology, and future development," said Kitagawa through an interpreter.
Kitagawa said the four-member Dream team had no real problems, mechanical or physical, on the hot and humid drive through Australia's red centre and past the famous Uluru (Ayers Rock).
However, he admitted with some chagrin that the team had taken a wrong turn on the highway on the last leg of the race and drove into oncoming traffic.
